content: Condensed Detachment, also referred to as Rule D, is a logical method used to derive the most general conclusion possible from two formal logical statements. This method was developed by the Irish logician Carew Meredith in the 1950s, drawing inspiration from the work of Łukasiewicz. The rule of detachment, in its basic form, states: If a proposition ( p ) is true, and ( p ) implies ( q ), then ( q ) must also be true. Condensed Detachment extends this principle further. It states: If ( p ) is true, and a second proposition ( r ) is given, then the most general result can be derived by applying substitutions to ( q ) and ( r ), followed by the standard rule of detachment. Substitutions ( A ) and ( B ), when applied to ( p ) and ( r ) respectively, are referred to as the unifiers of ( p ). These unifiers may yield expressions with varying numbers of free variables. Some unifying expressions are substitution instances of others. If one expression is a substitution instance of another (and not merely a renaming of variables), the latter is considered more general. When the most general unifier is used in Condensed Detachment, the resulting logical conclusion is the most general inference that can be made given the second expression. Since weaker inferences are merely substitution instances of the most general one, only the most general unifier is practically used. In certain logical systems, such as standard Propositional Calculus (PC), there exist defining axioms with the property of D-completeness. This means that any conclusion derivable through a sequence of uniform substitutions and Modus Ponens steps can either be achieved through a sequence of Condensed Detachment steps or is a substitution instance of something that can be derived in this way. For example, the logical expression: [ ((((A rightarrow B) rightarrow (neg C rightarrow neg D)) rightarrow C) rightarrow E) rightarrow ((E rightarrow A) rightarrow (D rightarrow A)) ] illustrates the application of such principles. Meredith observed that, since a given major premise and a given minor premise uniquely determine the conclusion (up to variable renaming), it is only necessary to specify which two statements are involved. This observation led to the development of D-notation for proofs. In this notation, the D operator represents Condensed Detachment and takes two arguments in a standard prefix notation string. For instance, the expression `D D 1 2 D 3 4` represents a Condensed Detachment step that uses the results of two prior Condensed Detachment steps. The first step involves axioms 1 and 2, while the second step involves axioms 3 and 4. This notation is not only used in some automated theorem provers but also occasionally appears in catalogs of proofs. The use of unification in Condensed Detachment predates the resolution techniques commonly employed in automated theorem proving.
